name: Bile Acid Malabsorption

prevalence.estimate: Up to 1% of general population; up to 25-33% of IBS-D patients

criteria.description: Objective evidence of bile acid malabsorption (SeHCAT retention < 15%, elevated serum C4, elevated fecal bile acids, or positive bile acid sequestrant trial)
Response to bile acid sequestrant therapy (cholestyramine, colesevelam)
History of ileal resection, Crohn's disease affecting ileum, cholecystectomy, or radiation enteritis

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Chronic diarrhea with objective evidence of bile acid malabsorption or clinical response to bile acid sequestrant trial.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Type 1: ileal disease/resection. Type 2: idiopathic (primary; defective FGF19 regulation). Type 3: secondary to other GI conditions (cholecystectomy, celiac, SIBO, post-radiation).

pathognomonic.notes: Often explosive, urgency-predominant; worse after fatty meals

common.notes: Due to urgency and watery stool consistency

occasional.notes: When bile acid pool is severely depleted

rare.symptomName: Fat-soluble vitamin deficiency (A, D, E, K)
rare.notes: In severe, long-standing cases with significant bile acid loss
From depleted bile acid pool altering bile composition
From bile acid irritation of perianal skin

laboratory: SeHCAT retention test: < 15% at 7 days (mild: 10-15%, moderate: 5-10%, severe: < 5%)
Elevated fecal bile acids (48-hour collection > 2,337 micromol/48h)
imaging: CT or MRI enterography to evaluate ileal disease (if Type 1 suspected)
No specific imaging findings for BAM itself
genetic: Variants in SLC10A2 (ileal bile acid transporter ASBT) in rare familial cases
FGF19 regulatory pathway alterations in Type 2 (idiopathic) BAM
other: Therapeutic trial of cholestyramine or colesevelam is commonly used as a diagnostic test
SeHCAT test is gold standard but not available in all countries (e.g., not available in USA)
Fasting serum C4 is most practical blood test where available

distinguishingFeatures: IBS-D lacks objective evidence of bile acid malabsorption on testing
Significant overlap: 25-33% of IBS-D patients may have BAM
Microscopic colitis diagnosed by colonic biopsies showing collagenous or lymphocytic pattern
Microscopic colitis responds to budesonide rather than bile acid sequestrants
Celiac disease confirmed by serology (anti-tTG) and duodenal biopsies
Celiac disease has villous atrophy and responds to gluten-free diet

redFlags: Bloody diarrhea (suggests alternative diagnosis such as IBD)
Significant weight loss (consider malignancy or severe malabsorption syndrome)
Nocturnal diarrhea with systemic symptoms (consider organic etiology beyond BAM)
references: Walters JR, et al. A new mechanism for bile acid diarrhea: defective feedback inhibition of bile acid biosynthesis. Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2009;7(11):1189-1194.

Wedlake L, et al. Systematic review: the prevalence of idiopathic bile acid malabsorption as diagnosed by SeHCAT scanning in patients with diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome. Aliment Pharmacol Ther. 2009;30(7):707-717.

Vijayvargiya P, et al. Bile acid deficiency in a subgroup of patients with irritable bowel syndrome with constipation based on biomarkers in serum and fecal samples. Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2018;16(4):522-527.
